sn47.7:1.1: This parable tells of a foolish monkey who gets stuck in a tar trap, reminiscent of “The Tarbaby and the Rabbit” story type. This has many instances worldwide. “Br’er Rabbit and the Tarbaby” was collected from stories told among black slaves in the US, and originates from Africa. Ja 55 tells of a warrior whose five weapons serve only to stick him to the coat of a _yakkha_. The Phillipine folk-tale Masoy and the Ape tells of an ape getting stuck in tar in the shape of a man. The current case is a little different, as there is no doll or mannikin.
sn47.7:1.4: The tar (_lepa_) was made from the sap of the banyan tree. | For _oḍḍenti_ (“set snare”) see [sn1.67:1.1](), [sn3.6:3.4](), [ja484:3.1](). | I feel the text is deficient here: we do not know on what the tar was smeared, nor why the monkey would grab it. When, later, we are told it is a banana tree (though the reading is uncertain), these questions are answered. There, the pronoun _tasmiṁyeva_ (“on that very”) implies that the banana tree had been mentioned before. I suspect it was mentioned here but has been lost.
sn47.7:2.12: The five points on which the monkey is stuck represent the five senses, trapping the monkey with greed.
sn47.7:2.13: In his note on this Sutta, Bodhi acknowledges the difficult reading _kaṭṭha-kataṅgāre_ and proposes the emendation _kaṭṭha-kaliṅgare_ based on the Buddhist Sanskrit _kāṣṭha-kaḍambara_. He then takes it to mean a block of wood, to which the hunter fastens the monkey before leaving with both monkey and block. This, however, creates several problems. Since both _kaṭṭha_ and _kaliṅgara_ mean “block of wood”, why the compound? Why does the hunter secure the monkey to the wood, when the whole point of the simile was that the monkey was stuck? Why read the verb _avassajjetvā_ as “having fastened” when the normal meaning of _avassajati_ is “release”, confirmed by the BJT reading _uddharitvā_, and agreeing with other occurrences of _yena kāmaṁ pakkamati_, which are preceded by someone being released ([mn66:10.1](), [an5.75:14.4](), [an8.14:7.1]())? And why would the hunter carry a log of wood out from such a remote region? I propose that _kaṭṭha-kataṅgāra_ is a corrupted form related to the Sanskrit _kāṣṭha-kadalī_, the wild plantain; perhaps the *Musa mannii*, a rare species found today in Arunchal Pradesh and sometimes known as the Indian Dwarf Banana. The hunter spears the trapped monkey while it is stuck to its favorite fruit tree, killing it, then pries it off and goes on his way.
